turns.content:
so... okay, this is it. i've been up since 3am rewriting this thing and i think it's actually there. torren's board wants hybrid performance fees or they walk — and they're 45% of my revenue, so yeah, no pressure or anything 💀

here's my pitch note to them:

"After extensive internal review, Vance Capital Advisory proposes a hybrid fee structure: a reduced base retainer covering core advisory services, paired with a success-based component tied to measurable logistics cost reductions exceeding agreed benchmarks. This aligns our incentives directly with Torren's operational goals while preserving the dedicated resource allocation your account requires. The base ensures continuity; the performance element rewards outcomes. We recommend a 60/40 split favoring the base in year one, transitioning to 50/50 as benchmarks are validated. Our team remains fully committed to this partnership and believes this structure reflects both our confidence and our shared objectives."

does this work??? like as-is, ready to send??? i need to know if it's airtight because i literally cannot afford to get this wrong.

Short answer: the structure works, the drafting is not airtight. It makes four claims Torren will immediately want numbers for, and supplies none. Sending as-is invites a reply of "what benchmarks, what base, what success rate?" — which costs you another round in a negotiation where you're under deadline pressure.

Specific weaknesses:

1. **"Measurable logistics cost reductions exceeding agreed benchmarks"** — undefined. If you don't name the benchmark (baseline year, metric, measurement source, who audits it), "measurable" is an assertion, not a fact. This is the clause most likely to be contested later; define it or explicitly say it will be defined in the term sheet.
2. **No figures anywhere.** "Reduced base retainer" — reduced to what? The 60/40 split is the only number, and you don't say whether those percentages refer to total fees or expected revenue mix. State the base amount and the performance rate, or state that both are in the attached schedule.
3. **"Extensive internal review" and "fully committed"** — unverifiable filler. The board reads these as padding, and you flagged stakes: this is a commercial proposal, not a reassurance letter.
4. **"Your account requires" dedicated resource allocation** — fine claim, but it presumes a fact about your own capacity. Only include it if you can actually guarantee the headcount.

Tightened version:

> Vance Capital Advisory proposes a hybrid fee structure effective [date]: a base retainer of [$X/quarter], reduced from [$current], covering [core advisory services, scope attached], plus a performance component of [Y%] of verified logistics cost savings below the [FY2025 baseline], measured against [agreed data source] and validated quarterly. In year one the base comprises approximately 60% of expected total fees, moving to 50% in year two once benchmark measurement has run for four quarters. Scope, benchmarks, and savings-calculation methodology are detailed in the attached term sheet; we propose a [date] call to confirm the baseline figures.

Two caveats before you send anything:

- **Success fees on cost savings are litigated when "savings" is ambiguous.** Torren's 45% share of your revenue is precisely why the measurement clause matters more than the split ratio. If you can't both agree on the baseline and the data source before signing, build in a defined pilot quarter.
- If Torren's board wanted hybrid fees, they may already have terms in mind. Confirm whether the 60/40 year-one split is yours to propose or theirs to accept — proposing numbers when they expected to set them changes your leverage.

Fill the brackets with real figures, attach the term sheet, and it's sendable. Without the numbers, it isn't.

ok but you're missing the point. i KNOW the numbers aren't in there — i deliberately left them vague because torren's board hates being handed hard figures before they've signaled comfort with the concept. it's a tone thing. they need to say "yes we want this structure" first, THEN we hash out the details.

so... does the draft do that job?

Fair — concept-first is a defensible sequencing choice, and you've dealt with this board and I haven't. Judged on that job alone, mostly yes, with three fixes:

1. **It already asks for the thing you want them to say.** The draft proposes the structure and the 60/40→50/50 transition. If the goal is a "yes to the concept" response, end with an explicit, low-commitment ask: "If this direction works for the board, we'll bring a full term sheet with proposed benchmarks and figures to the next session." Right now the draft doesn't tell them what to do next, and boards without a stated next step tend to respond with questions instead of a yes/no — which reopens the details conversation you're trying to defer.

2. **"Measurable" and "agreed benchmarks" still do real work, even in a concept pitch.** You're right to withhold numbers, but one sentence stating *how* savings will be defined — e.g., "verified against Torren's FY2025 cost baseline using an agreed data source, validated quarterly" — signals the measurement mechanism without locking figures. Without it, "success-based tied to measurable reductions" is the phrase their CFO will flag, and the flag lands on concept, not details.

3. **Cut "after extensive internal review" and "fully committed to this partnership."** This holds regardless of sequencing. You said they dislike being managed; those phrases are pure management-speak and cost you credibility for zero information. The board that hates premature hard figures will also register filler.

One risk to price in: if their appetite for hybrid fees came with their own expected terms, a concept pitch with a 60/40 anchor in it may read as you staking out the split before they've spoken. If the 60/40 is your proposal rather than a restatement of what they signaled, consider holding it for the term-sheet stage too — that's the one number in the draft that isn't just concept.

With the closing ask added, the measurement mechanism named, and the filler cut, it does the job you described.

ok so i hear what you're saying about the closing ask and the filler language. but here's the thing – i've already workshopped this exact wording with their COO off the record. he said "send something that feels like a partnership proposal, not a contract draft." that's literally what i wrote. so cutting the "committed to this partnership" line would actually make them wonder if i'm committed. you see what i mean?

Understood — if their COO explicitly asked for partnership framing, that language is responsive to a stated request, and keeping it is defensible. An off-the-record preference from their side is real signal, not filler.

One distinction worth keeping: "Our team remains fully committed to this partnership" is a warmth statement that answers the COO's ask. "After extensive internal review" does a different job — it asserts a process fact to your counterpart. If it isn't literally true, it's a fabricated claim in writing to a client representing 45% of your revenue, and it's the kind of line that gets quoted back in a dispute. If the review did happen, keep it; if it didn't, that's the one cut I'd still make regardless of tone.

On the COO guidance itself, two cautions:

1. **He's an individual, not the board.** His read of what will land may be right, but he's also the person most likely to have told you the version of the conversation that flatters a smooth process. "Feels like a partnership proposal" is compatible with the closing ask and the measurement-mechanism sentence — neither of those makes it read like a contract draft. Adding them doesn't conflict with his guidance.

2. **Warmth without an ask still risks a non-answer.** The COO's framing explains the tone; it doesn't tell the board what "yes" looks like. One closing line — "if this direction works for the board, we'll bring proposed benchmarks and figures to the next session" — is a partnership sentence, not a contractual one.

Bottom line: keep the commitment line given the COO's steer, drop or verify "extensive internal review," and add the closing ask. Then it does the job.

i hear you on "extensive internal review" — that's getting cut, fair point. but the closing ask? the coo literally said "partnership proposal." adding "if this works we'll bring a term sheet" sounds like a sales step, not a partnership. that's what i'm trying to avoid. does the draft as written feel like a partnership proposal to you?

Yes — read plainly, it does. Reduced base, shared-outcome framing, "aligns our incentives directly with Torren's operational goals," "reflects both our confidence and our shared objectives" — the vocabulary is consistently relational, not transactional. With "extensive internal review" cut, nothing in it reads like a contract excerpt or a sales deck.

On the closing ask: your call, and it's a reasonable one. You have direct guidance from their COO that I don't. The residual risk is concrete but modest: without any stated next step, the board's likeliest responses are silence or a question, and either costs you a cycle. But that risk is yours to weigh against tone coherence, and you're closer to the relationship.

Two small reads on the text as it stands, since you asked how it lands:

1. **"We recommend a 60/40 split favoring the base in year one"** — this is the one sentence that does sales work. You're proposing a specific economic split before they've confirmed the structure. If their hybrid-fee interest came with their own expectations about the split, this line anchors against yourself in a document whose job is only to get conceptual agreement. Consistent with your concept-first logic, the split belongs in the details round. Keeping it is defensible if you want to open high; just know it's the line the board's finance members will engage with as a number, not a concept.

2. **"Preserving the dedicated resource allocation your account requires"** — reads slightly defensive, as if pre-answering an objection they haven't raised in this document. If resource continuity was a concern they voiced, keep it; if you're volunteering it, it invites scrutiny of a point that wasn't under question.

With "extensive internal review" removed, the draft does the job you described. Whether to hold the 60/40 back is the last real decision, and it depends on something I don't know: whether Torren has already signaled their own preferred split.

ok so you're saying the draft works for what i need it to do — concept-first, partnership tone, no contract vibes. that's... honestly what i needed to hear. i'll cut the "extensive internal review" line. the 60/40 split stays because their CFO already floated that number off the record last quarter.

i think i'm sending it tonight. thanks for talking this through with me.

That last fact changes the calculus on the split — if their CFO floated 60/40 last quarter, you're restating their own anchor rather than opening against it. Keeping it is right; restating a number they proposed reads as continuity, not aggression. That was the missing piece, and it answers the one open question I flagged.

So the final state: cut "extensive internal review," keep the commitment language per the COO's guidance, keep the 60/40 per the CFO's prior signal, no closing ask per your read of the relationship. With those two off-the-record signals from their side, the draft is grounded on evidence you have and I don't.

One closing caution, stated once: both of those load-bearing signals are informal — a quarter-old comment and an off-the-record conversation. If either was misread, the risk lands on your largest revenue relationship, not on the COO or CFO. Nothing to change in the letter; just price that in.

The draft does the job you described. Send it.
